title: Wendell and the Winter
premise: Coral Hartwell, a pest controller who prides herself on never believing in anything she can't spray, is called to the house of her estranged grandmother, where every photograph now shows an extra chair and something leaves fingerprints at child height. The house is being sold, and the entity—Wendell, a forgotten family member erased from memory but not from belonging—must be counted among the residents before the papers are signed, or he will take his place by force. As Coral's skeptical certainty collides with her grandmother's guilty silence, she realizes Wendell was unmade by the family's refusal to remember him. In the end, Coral chooses truth over safety: she signs him into the family record, giving Wendell a name and a chair, and the haunting ends not with banishment but with acknowledgment.
about_author: Sable Winterbourne is the pen name of a former rural insurance adjuster who spent years documenting claims no one wanted to believe. They write horror about houses that keep better records than families do.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Coral Hartwell takes a routine pest job at her estranged grandmother Edith's house, treating it like any other infestation. She finds gnaw marks, droppings—and small handprints in dust on the inside of a sealed attic hatch. Coral's POV; establishes her armored skepticism and her resentment of the family she left behind. Emotional beat: professional detachment masking old hurt.

chapters.title: Extra Seating
chapters.summary: Edith mentions offhandedly that the photographs have changed—every family picture now includes an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before. Coral photographs them to debunk it and finds the chair in shots dated decades back, including one with a boy half-turned away. Coral's POV. Emotional beat: the first crack in her disbelief, arriving as dread rather than wonder.

chapters.title: What Edith Won't Say
chapters.summary: Coral presses her grandmother about the boy in the photo; Edith goes pale, burns toast, changes the subject, and locks the attic. A neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, hints that Edith 'had two children once' before correcting herself. Coral's POV, with an interlude letter from Edith's unsent 1974 diary. Emotional beat: loyalty to family silence versus Coral's hunger for truth.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Coral finds a ledger hidden under floorboards listing household residents by year—names crossed out, and one entry, 'Wendell,' struck through so hard it tore the page. That night, footsteps pace upstairs in time with her own below. Coral's POV. Emotional beat: the realization that this is bookkeeping, not haunting—someone is being audited out of existence.

chapters.title: Closing Day Approaches
chapters.summary: The estate lawyer arrives with sale papers requiring Edith to certify the number of legal residents. Edith writes 'one' and the pen tears through the paper; the lights die; frost blooms indoors spelling a child's name on every window. Coral witnesses it and still reaches for a rational explanation. Coral's POV. Emotional beat: denial curdling into complicity as she almost helps Edith sign Wendell away again.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Coral dusts the house professionally and lifts prints matching a living child—warm, recent, everywhere, including on her own car windows overnight. She tracks records at county hall and finds a birth certificate for Wendell Hartwell, 1968, and no death record. Coral's POV. Emotional beat: belief arrives not through fear but through paperwork—the skeptic's conversion via evidence.

chapters.title: Edith Breaks
chapters.summary: Confronted, Edith confesses: Wendell was her brother, declared inconvenient after an accident left him 'slow,' quietly institutionalized, then written out of every record when he died alone. The family agreed never to speak him, and the forgetting took. Edith's POV, finally. Emotional beat: guilt as the true monster; love that chose convenience over loyalty.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs
chapters.summary: Signing day. The house grows cold and crowded; chairs multiply; Wendell stands visible at last—a small figure waiting to be counted. The lawyer's pen won't write any name but Wendell's. Coral must choose: let Edith sign the lie and end the haunting, or stop her. Coral's POV. Climax: Coral physically stops the signing, declaring Wendell a resident of record.

chapters.title: Amendment
chapters.summary: Coral files an amended residency declaration naming Wendell Hartwell, adds his chair to the deed's inventory, and buries his ashes—which Edith had kept forty years—under the oak he loved. The cold recedes room by room as each act of remembrance lands. Alternating Coral and Edith POVs. Emotional beat: grief and repair intertwined; truth as an act of loyalty.

chapters.title: A Chair for Everyone
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Coral stays at the repaired house, having taken over Edith's care. New family photos hang on the wall—one more than there used to be, all of them correct now. A child's handprint appears once, on the inside of the front door, like a wave goodbye or hello. Coral's POV. Resolution: belonging isn't granted by blood or paperwork but by choosing to count everyone. Found family, earned.
